blocks.text: 1. Pruning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446426806-659978054.png

TensorRT's own closing recap, already covered in TensorRT, pointed forward here. Pruning, a technique that removes unneeded weights to shrink and speed up a model, tackles model size directly at the source.
It genuinely identifies and deletes connections that contribute little to the network's own actual output, a process explored in full throughout this topic.

This connects back to TensorRT's own closing recap, already covered in TensorRT. Pruning was genuinely previewed there as removing unneeded weights to shrink and speed up a model, briefly described in that earlier topic.

3. Recapping Redundancy In Large Models
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446426806-252328466.png
This connects back to large models, already covered generally across this course. Genuinely large, trained networks often genuinely contain far more weights than are genuinely strictly necessary.
Many genuinely individual connections genuinely contribute very little to the final, real output, the exact real observation motivating pruning explored throughout the rest of this topic.
4. Identifying Low Importance Weights
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446426806-610123927.png

This connects back to recapping redundancy in large models, already covered in this topic. Pruning genuinely identifies which specific weights genuinely matter least, often using their own magnitude as a simple signal.
Genuinely weights close to zero genuinely tend to contribute little to the network's own final output, a genuinely practical, easy-to-compute criterion explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.text: 5. Removing The Selected Weights
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446426806-906820441.png
This connects back to identifying low importance weights, already covered in this topic. Those genuinely selected low-importance weights then genuinely get set to zero or removed entirely.
This genuinely shrinks the effective size of the network without genuinely changing its own overall architecture, the exact core action explored throughout the rest of this topic.
6. Structured Versus Unstructured Pruning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446426806-84619925.png
This connects back to removing the selected weights, already covered in this topic. Unstructured pruning genuinely removes individual weights scattered throughout the network.
Structured pruning genuinely removes entire genuinely organized groups instead, like whole neurons or filters, a genuinely important distinction explored throughout the rest of this topic.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This distinction, already covered in this topic, directly explains why structured pruning genuinely tends to produce more real-world speedups: removing whole neurons or filters, already covered generally in Convolutional Neural Networks, is genuinely easier for hardware to exploit than scattered, individual weights.

blocks.text: 7. Fine Tuning After Pruning
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785446426806-351589162.png

This connects back to structured versus unstructured pruning, already covered in this topic. Removing weights genuinely tends to hurt accuracy somewhat, so pruning is genuinely usually followed by a short fine-tuning step.

Already covered generally in Full Fine-Tuning, this genuinely lets the remaining weights adjust and recover lost accuracy, a genuinely important, standard practice explored throughout the rest of this topic.
8. Iterative Pruning

This connects back to fine tuning after pruning, already covered in this topic. Rather than genuinely pruning aggressively all at once, many pipelines genuinely repeat prune-then-fine-tune in several smaller rounds.

This genuinely gradually reaches a genuinely much smaller model while genuinely preserving more of its original accuracy, a genuinely gentler, more effective overall approach explored throughout the rest of this topic.

10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates identifying and removing low-magnitude weights, already covered in this topic, from a small set of weights.

code.content:
weights = [0.85, -0.02, 0.4, 0.01, -0.6, 0.005, 0.3, -0.008]

def prune_by_magnitude(weights, threshold=0.05):
    # already covered as identifying low importance weights in this topic
    pruned = [w if abs(w) >= threshold else 0.0 for w in weights]
    return pruned

pruned_weights = prune_by_magnitude(weights)
print(f"Original weights (already covered in this topic): {weights}")
print(f"Pruned weights (already covered as removing the selected weights in this topic): {pruned_weights}")

# already covered as structured versus unstructured pruning in this topic
num_pruned = sum(1 for w in pruned_weights if w == 0.0)
print(f"\nWeights pruned (already covered in this topic): {num_pruned} out of {len(weights)}")
print(f"Remaining non-zero weights: {len(weights) - num_pruned}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows weights with small magnitudes genuinely set to zero while larger weights genuinely remain untouched, exactly the magnitude-based pruning criterion already covered in this topic.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Pruning removes unneeded weights to shrink and speed up a model.
Large, trained networks often contain far more weights than strictly necessary.
Pruning identifies low-importance weights, often using magnitude close to zero as a signal.
Selected low-importance weights get set to zero or removed entirely, shrinking the network.
Unstructured pruning removes scattered individual weights; structured pruning removes whole groups.
Structured pruning tends to produce more real-world speedups, since hardware exploits it more easily.
Removing weights hurts accuracy somewhat, so pruning is usually followed by fine-tuning.
Iterative pruning repeats prune-then-fine-tune in smaller rounds, preserving more accuracy overall.
Next up: Distillation, another technique for producing a smaller, faster model.
